claims.text: What the image looks like Hyperdensity in basal cisterns / Sylvian fissure / sulci → subarachnoid hemorrhage
claims.quote: Hyperdensity in basal cisterns / Sylvian fissure / sulci Subarachnoid hemorrhage

claims.text: Example CT: blood in the sulci; blood is often also seen in the ventricles
claims.quote: This CT scan in a patient with a subarachnoid hemorrhage shows blood in the sulci (arrow). Blood is often also seen in the ventricles.

claims.text: Buzzword: star/pentagon hyperdensity in the basal cisterns on head CT → aneurysmal SAH
claims.quote: Star/pentagon hyperdensity in basal cisterns Head CT Aneurysmal SAH

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Confirm it is non-contrast (so blood/calcium is not confused with contrast)
claims.quote: Confirm non-contrast (so blood/calcium not confused with contrast).

claims.text: Symmetry: gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns
claims.quote: Symmetry - gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns.

claims.text: Blood: look for hyperdensity 60-80 HU (epidural / subdural / SAH / IPH / IVH)
claims.quote: Blood - look for hyperdensity 60-80 HU (epidural / subdural / SAH / IPH / IVH).

claims.text: Brain: gray-white preservation; look for sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift
claims.quote: Brain - gray-white preservation, sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift.

claims.text: Cisterns: basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk
claims.quote: Cisterns - basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk.

claims.text: Ventricles: symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus
claims.quote: Ventricles - symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus.

claims.text: Noncontrast CT is performed within 6 hours of symptom onset; in this time frame it has very high sensitivity
claims.quote: Noncontrast CT is performed within 6 hours of symptom onset. When performed within this time frame, this test has very high sensitivity.

claims.text: False-negative CT occurs if the volume of blood is small or with profound anemia (blood isodense with brain tissue)
claims.quote: False-negative results occur if the volume of blood is small or if there is profound anemia such that blood is isodense with brain tissue.

claims.text: Causes Her chart: aneurysmal; ACom most common
claims.quote: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal; ACom most common)

claims.text: Bleeding between the arachnoid and pia mater; head trauma is the most common cause overall (traumatic SAH is usually considered a separate disorder); spontaneous SAH usually results from ruptured aneurysms, with a congenital saccular (berry) aneurysm the cause in approximately 85%
claims.quote: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is bleeding between the arachnoid and pia mater. In general, head trauma is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage, but traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is usually considered a separate disorder. Spontaneous (primary) subarachnoid hemorrhage usually results from ruptured aneurysms. A congenital intracranial saccular or berry aneurysm is the cause in approximately 85% of patients.

claims.text: Aneurysmal hemorrhage may occur at any age but is most common from age 40 to 65; less common causes are mycotic aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, amyloid deposition and bleeding disorders
claims.quote: Aneurysmal hemorrhage may occur at any age but is most common from age 40 to 65. Less common causes are mycotic aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, amyloid deposition, and bleeding disorders.

claims.text: Blood causes a chemical meningitis that commonly raises ICP for days or weeks; secondary vasospasm may cause focal ischemia (approximately 25% develop TIA or ischemic stroke signs), with vasospasm and infarction risk highest between 72 hours and 10 days; secondary acute hydrocephalus is common; rebleeding sometimes occurs, most often within 7 days
claims.quote: Blood in the subarachnoid space causes a chemical meningitis that commonly increases intracranial pressure for days or a few weeks. Secondary vasospasm may cause focal brain ischemia; approximately 25% of patients develop signs of a transient ischemic attack (TIA) or ischemic stroke. Brain edema is maximal and risk of vasospasm and subsequent infarction (called angry brain) is highest between 72 hours and 10 days. Secondary acute hydrocephalus is also common. A 2nd rupture (rebleeding) sometimes occurs, most often within 7 days.

claims.text: Symptoms Her chart: 'Thunderclap headache'
claims.quote: 'Thunderclap headache'

claims.text: Headache is usually severe, peaking within seconds; patients often describe it as "the worst headache in their life"; loss of consciousness may follow, usually immediately but sometimes not for several hours
claims.quote: Headache is usually severe, peaking within seconds. Patients often describe it as "the worst headache in their life." Loss of consciousness may follow, usually immediately but sometimes not for several hours.

claims.text: Usually the neck is not stiff initially (unless the cerebellar tonsils herniate); within 24 hours chemical meningitis causes moderate to marked meningismus, vomiting and sometimes bilateral extensor plantar responses
claims.quote: Usually, the neck is not stiff initially unless the cerebellar tonsils herniate. However, within 24 hours, chemical meningitis causes moderate to marked meningismus, vomiting, and sometimes bilateral extensor plantar responses.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: CTA for aneurysm; nimodipine; coil/clip
claims.quote: CTA for aneurysm; nimodipine; coil/clip.

claims.text: Her chart: if CT negative > 6 h post-onset → LP for xanthochromia
claims.quote: If CT negative >6 h post-onset → LP for xanthochromia

claims.text: If SAH is suspected but not identified by neuroimaging, or imaging is not immediately available, lumbar puncture is performed; LP is contraindicated if increased ICP is suspected (a sudden CSF pressure drop may cause further bleeding)
claims.quote: If subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected clinically but not identified by neuroimaging, or if neuroimaging is not immediately available, lumbar puncture is performed. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated if increased intracranial pressure is suspected because the sudden decrease in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure may lessen the tamponade of a clot on the ruptured aneurysm, causing further bleeding.

claims.text: CSF findings suggesting SAH: numerous RBCs, xanthochromia, increased pressure
claims.quote: CSF findings suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage include Numerous red blood cells (RBCs) Xanthochromia Increased pressure

claims.text: Approximately 6 hours or more after SAH, RBCs crenate and lyse, giving a xanthochromic CSF supernatant; these findings usually indicate the SAH preceded the lumbar puncture
claims.quote: Approximately 6 hours or more after a subarachnoid hemorrhage, RBCs become crenated and lyse, resulting in a xanthochromic CSF supernatant and visible crenated RBCs (noted during microscopic CSF examination); these findings usually indicate that subarachnoid hemorrhage preceded the lumbar puncture.

claims.text: If CT or LP shows bleeding, angiography confirms it and finds the aneurysm or AVM; cerebral angiography is more invasive than MRA or CTA but gives more information, though CTA has largely replaced it for diagnosing aneurysms within the skull
claims.quote: If bleeding is indicated by CT or lumbar puncture, angiography is performed to confirm the diagnosis and to identify the site of the aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation causing the bleeding. Cerebral angiography is more invasive than MRA or CTA but provides more information. However, CTA has largely replaced cerebral angiography for the diagnosis of aneurysms within the skull.

claims.text: All 4 arteries (2 carotid and 2 vertebral) should be injected, because up to 20% of patients (mostly women) have multiple aneurysms
claims.quote: All 4 arteries (2 carotid and 2 vertebral arteries) should be injected because up to 20% of patients (mostly women) have multiple aneurysms.

claims.text: Treat in a comprehensive stroke center whenever possible
claims.quote: Patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage should be treated in a comprehensive stroke center whenever possible.

claims.text: Treat hypertension only if mean arterial pressure is > 130 mm Hg or systolic BP > 160 mm Hg; maintain euvolemia and titrate IV nicardipine as for intracerebral hemorrhage
claims.quote: Hypertension should be treated only if mean arterial pressure is > 130 mm Hg or systolic blood pressure (BP) is > 160 mm Hg; euvolemia is maintained, and IV nicardipine is titrated as for intracerebral hemorrhage (1).

claims.text: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet medications are contraindicated
claims.quote: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet medications are contraindicated.

claims.text: Nimodipine prevents vasospasm, but BP must stay in range (usually mean arterial pressure 70 to 130 mm Hg and systolic 120 to 185 mm Hg)
claims.quote: Vasospasm is prevented by giving nimodipine, but BP needs to be maintained in the desirable range (usually considered to be a mean arterial pressure of 70 to 130 mm Hg and a systolic pressure of 120 to 185 mm Hg).

claims.text: If clinical signs of acute hydrocephalus occur, ventricular drainage should be considered
claims.quote: If clinical signs of acute hydrocephalus occur, ventricular drainage should be considered.

claims.text: Aneurysms are occluded to reduce rebleeding: detachable endovascular coils can be inserted during angiography, or, if the aneurysm is accessible, surgery can clip or stent it (especially with an evacuable hematoma or acute hydrocephalus)
claims.quote: Aneurysms are occluded to reduce risk of rebleeding. Detachable endovascular coils can be inserted during angiography to occlude the aneurysm. Alternatively, if the aneurysm is accessible, surgery to clip or stent the aneurysm can be performed, especially for patients with an evacuable hematoma or acute hydrocephalus.
